sections.name: General Knowledge / Current Affairs of India and Goa
Core: Organon of Medicine and Homoeopathic Philosophy

p1.title: Passage 1
paras: Before piped water, a village's supply was a matter of knowing where the hill held its rain. Springs emerged where the laterite met a harder rock beneath, and around each one generations built a small tank, a stone spout and a channel leading to the fields below. Maintaining them was nobody's job and therefore everybody's. Before each monsoon the families who drew from a spring cleared its channel, because a blocked channel was their own dry field.

The pipeline ended this dependence, and with it the maintenance. Water now came from a reservoir forty kilometres away, at the turn of a tap, and the spring became a place where children bathed and nobody cleaned. In most villages the channel has silted up and the tank holds a film of green water and plastic.

The loss is felt only on certain days. When a pump fails or a main bursts, the taps run dry for a week and the tanker arrives late. The older residents remember that the spring is still flowing, as it always has, into a tank that can no longer hold what it gives. Reviving these works is cheap by the standards of any water scheme. The difficulty is not money. It is that a community looks after what it relies on, and a source that is needed five days a year is hard to care about on the other three hundred and sixty.

p2.title: Passage 2
paras: In most organisations bad news travels upward slowly, and arrives smaller than it set out. The clerk who notices that a scheme's figures do not add up mentions it carefully to the head clerk, who mentions it more carefully to the officer, who decides that it need not be mentioned further until it has been looked into. Each has softened the message slightly, and each has behaved as a prudent person would. By the time the head of the department hears of the matter, it is a rumour that something may need attention at some point.

The cause is not dishonesty. It is that messengers are judged along with their messages. A subordinate who brings a problem is asked why it was allowed to happen, while one who brings nothing is assumed to have nothing to bring. People learn quickly which of these is the safer habit.

A head of office who wants the truth early must therefore make it cheap to tell. This means asking for bad news in so many words, thanking the person who brings it before asking who is to blame, and never letting a meeting end on the phrase 'everything is under control' without one question about what is not. The reward is unglamorous: small problems heard of on Monday that would otherwise have been large ones by Friday. Offices that seem to be struck by sudden crises have usually had the news for weeks, at a level where nobody felt able to pass it on.

questions.q: Why did families clear the channel of a spring before each monsoon?
opts: Their own fields depended on it
The panchayat paid them to do so
questions.why: A blocked channel was their own dry field.

questions.q: 'Nobody's job and therefore everybody's' means that:
opts: no one was appointed, so all the users shared the work
only the eldest family did the work
questions.why: With no one employed for it, those who drew from the spring maintained it themselves.

questions.q: What happened to the springs after piped water arrived?
opts: They were closed by the authorities
They were connected to the pipeline
They were neglected and their channels silted up
questions.why: The pipeline ended the dependence and with it the maintenance; channels silted and tanks filled with rubbish.

questions.q: According to the passage, when is the loss of the old system felt?
opts: When children bathe in the tank
questions.why: The loss is felt when a pump fails or a main bursts and the taps run dry.

questions.q: What does the author identify as the main difficulty in reviving the old works?
opts: People do not maintain a source they seldom need
questions.why: The difficulty is not money: a source needed five days a year is hard to care about on the other days.

questions.q: According to the first paragraph, as bad news moves upward it becomes:
questions.why: Bad news travels upward slowly and arrives smaller than it set out.

questions.q: 'Each has behaved as a prudent person would' implies that softening the message is:
questions.why: The author says the cause is not dishonesty; each person acted cautiously.

questions.q: Why do subordinates learn to bring nothing?
opts: Those who report problems are questioned, while those who report nothing are not
They are too busy to report
questions.why: The one who brings a problem is asked why it happened; the one who brings nothing is assumed to have nothing to bring.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT among the author's suggestions to a head of office?
opts: Asking for bad news in so many words
Thanking the person who brings it
Punishing staff who report problems late
Questioning the claim that everything is under control
questions.why: The author's suggestions all make bad news cheaper to tell. Punishment is not among them.

questions.q: The last sentence suggests that 'sudden' crises are often:
opts: problems that were known lower down but not passed up
questions.why: Such offices have usually had the news for weeks, at a level where nobody felt able to pass it on.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: The work is ______ difficult for a beginner to do.
questions.why: The pattern 'too + adjective + to + verb' shows that something cannot be done.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: He asked me ______ I had seen the circular.
questions.why: A reported yes/no question is introduced by 'whether' or 'if'.

questions.q: Choose the passive voice of: Who wrote this note?
opts: By whom this note was written?
By whom is this note written?
By whom was this note written?
questions.why: The simple past passive is was + past participle, and 'who' becomes 'by whom'.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Ten kilometres ______ a long distance to walk.
questions.why: A distance treated as a single amount takes a singular verb.

questions.q: Which part of the sentence contains an error? She is confident (A) / to win (B) / the first prize (C) / this year (D).
questions.why: 'Confident' is followed by 'of' and an -ing form: confident of winning.

questions.q: In which state will India’s first underwater museum and artificial coral reef be developed?
questions.why: Off Sindhudurg, Maharashtra, using a decommissioned warship. GPSC CBRT, Jun 2025.

questions.q: Which state launched the ‘Mee Bhoomi–Blockchain’ pilot for tamper-proof land records?
questions.why: Mee Bhoomi is Andhra Pradesh's land-records portal. GPSC CBRT, Sep 2026.

questions.q: Which state is known as the “Spice Garden of India”?
questions.why: Kerala. GPSC CBRT, Feb 2026.

questions.q: Which ministry signed an MoU with ICAR-CMFRI to implement the Matsya Shakti project?
questions.why: GPSC's key: the Ministry of Minority Affairs, for minority fishing communities. GPSC CBRT, Sep 2025.

questions.q: Which state announced India’s first AI university?
questions.why: Maharashtra, in 2025. GPSC CBRT, Mar 2025.

questions.q: On which date is Armed Forces Flag Day observed in India?
questions.why: 7 December, since 1949. GPSC CBRT, Dec 2024.

questions.q: Who won the FIDE World Junior (Under-20) Girls' Chess Championship in 2024?
questions.why: Divya Deshmukh, in Gujarat, June 2024. GPSC CBRT, Jul 2024.

questions.q: When is World Radio Day celebrated?
questions.why: 13 February, the day UN Radio began in 1946. GPSC CBRT, Mar 2024.

questions.q: Who became the first woman Director General of Police of Maharashtra?
questions.why: Rashmi Shukla, January 2024. GPSC CBRT, Feb 2024.

questions.q: Which country takes part in the joint army exercise Harimau Shakti with India?
questions.why: Harimau ('tiger') Shakti is the India–Malaysia exercise. GPSC CBRT, Nov 2023.

questions.q: Find the next number in the series: 8, 27, 64, 125, ?
questions.why: These are the cubes of 2, 3, 4 and 5. The next is 6 cubed, 216.

questions.q: Which letter is exactly midway between G and S in the English alphabet?
questions.why: G is the 7th letter and S the 19th. Midway is the 13th letter, M.

questions.q: If CLERK is written as DMFSL in a certain code, how is JUDGE written?
questions.why: Each letter moves one place forward: J-K, U-V, D-E, G-H, E-F.

questions.q: Thermometer is to temperature as seismograph is to:
questions.why: A seismograph records the ground movement caused by earthquakes.

questions.q: Q and R are brother and sister. P is Q's son and S is R's son. How is P related to S?
questions.why: The children of a brother and a sister are cousins.

questions.q: Starting from point X, Raju walks 6 km north, then 8 km east, then 6 km south. How far is he from X?
questions.why: The 6 km north and 6 km south cancel out, leaving him 8 km east of X.

questions.q: A, B and C can do a work in 20, 30 and 60 days. In how many days can A do it if B and C help him every third day?
questions.why: Per 3 days: 3/20 + 1/30 + 1/60 = 12/60 = 1/5 of the work, so 15 days. GPSC CBRT, Mar 2025.

questions.q: Which word does NOT belong with the others?
questions.why: The first three mean 'of little importance'. GPSC CBRT, Sep 2025.

questions.q: Statement: "The government should immediately tighten regulation of pharmaceutical advertising to protect public health." Which assumption is inherent?
opts: Such advertising now misleads the public or poses a health risk
Regulation is the only way to protect public health
The government has all the resources needed
Public health is deteriorating because of such advertising
questions.why: The call for urgent regulation presumes a present risk. B and D are too strong. GPSC CBRT, Jun 2025.

questions.q: Identify the next term: 1, 2, 6, 42, 1806, …
questions.why: Each term is n × (n + 1) of the previous: 1806 × 1807 = 3263442. GPSC CBRT, Jun 2025.

questions.q: In 1835 Hahnemann moved to Paris after marrying:
questions.why: His second wife, the French painter Melanie d'Hervilly, persuaded him to move to Paris.

questions.q: Hahnemann's 'The Chronic Diseases' first appeared in:
questions.why: The first volumes were published in 1828; a second, enlarged edition followed from 1835.

questions.q: The sixth edition of the Organon was translated into English in 1922 by:
questions.why: Dudgeon translated the fifth edition; Boericke translated the sixth.

questions.q: How many aphorisms does the sixth edition of the Organon contain?
questions.why: The sixth edition has 291 aphorisms; the fifth had 294.

questions.q: The word 'homoeopathy' first appeared in Hahnemann's writings in:
questions.why: He introduced the term in an 1807 essay in Hufeland's Journal.

questions.q: Roberts' 'The Principles and Art of Cure by Homoeopathy' was first published in:
questions.why: Kent's lectures appeared in 1900, the sixth Organon in 1921 and Close's Genius in 1924.

questions.q: According to §18, the sole indication guiding the choice of the remedy is:
opts: the totality of symptoms, with its accompanying circumstances
questions.why: §18: the sum of all the symptoms and circumstances is the sole indication.

questions.q: According to §21, the curative power of medicines can be known only through:
opts: their power to alter the health of healthy persons
questions.why: §21: their healing power is shown only by the changes they produce in healthy people.

questions.q: When two similar diseases meet in the body (§43-46), the stronger one:
opts: unites with it into a complex disease
questions.why: §43-46: a stronger similar disease extinguishes the weaker, as cowpox protects against smallpox.

questions.q: A new, stronger dissimilar disease attacks a person who already has a disease (§38). The older disease:
opts: is suspended until the new one has run its course
questions.why: §38: the stronger dissimilar disease suspends the older one, which returns afterwards.

questions.q: Which symptoms does §153 say should be chiefly kept in view when choosing the remedy?
opts: The striking, singular, uncommon and peculiar symptoms
The common symptoms of the disease
questions.why: §153: the characteristic symptoms must correspond most closely to the medicine.

questions.q: Hahnemann classed mental diseases (§210) as:
questions.why: §210: the so-called mental diseases are one-sided diseases in which the mental change dominates.

questions.q: During a proving, §124 requires each medicine to be:
opts: mixed with another to test its effects
given alone and perfectly pure, unmixed with any foreign substance
given only in the crude form
questions.why: §124: only a pure, single substance gives a true picture of its effects.

questions.q: According to §138, the symptoms that appear during a proving are:
opts: ignored unless confirmed in the sick
recorded only if they are pathological
questions.why: §138: all the ailments that occur during the action of the medicine come from it, provided the prover is healthy and careful.

questions.q: Which is NOT one of the three sources of symptoms named in §6 and §84?
opts: The textbook description of the disease
questions.why: The picture is drawn from the patient, the people around him and the physician's own observation.

questions.q: According to §99, acute cases are easier to investigate than chronic ones because:
opts: the symptoms are recent and fresh in memory
questions.why: §99: the phenomena of a recent disease are still fresh in the patient's and attendants' minds.

questions.q: If an ailment seems to come from a cause the patient may hide, such as grief or shame (§93), the physician should:
opts: enquire discreetly, if necessary from the relatives
questions.why: §93: such causes must be ascertained by skilful questioning or private enquiry.

questions.q: In Kent's observations, 'full-time amelioration of symptoms, yet no special relief to the patient' means:
opts: the patient can only be palliated, because of hidden organic disease
questions.why: Kent's seventh observation: symptoms improve but the patient does not, pointing to latent organic disease.

questions.q: Kent's first observation, prolonged aggravation and final decline of the patient, indicates:
opts: an incurable case: the remedy was too deep or the potency too high
questions.why: The vital force cannot react; destructive changes are present.

questions.q: After the first prescription the patient is steadily improving. The right course is to:
opts: wait, and not repeat or change while improvement continues
questions.why: A remedy that is acting is left alone. Kent: when in doubt, wait.

questions.q: Discharges with a fish-brine odour are characteristic of which miasm?
questions.why: Offensive, fish-brine discharges are a sycotic keynote.

questions.q: Which nosodes are the chief anti-tubercular remedies?
questions.why: Tuberculinum and Bacillinum are the tubercular nosodes.

questions.q: Psoric complaints are typically relieved by:
opts: the appearance of natural discharges or eruptions
questions.why: Psora is relieved when eruptions or natural discharges appear.

questions.q: Which tissue change is characteristic of the syphilitic miasm?
questions.why: Syphilis destroys tissue: ulcers, necrosis and bone involvement.

questions.q: How many chronic miasms did Hahnemann describe?
questions.why: Psora, syphilis and sycosis. The tubercular diathesis was described by later authors.
